2: At the end of the month, your I S S O needs to show an assessor three things.
That every identity finding was owned, clocked, re-read and closed.
That nothing was edited after it closed.
And that nothing was quietly dropped.
Ticket history and screenshots don't prove that.
A ticket shows a status, not a re-read.
And neither one can show an edit that left no trace, or a record that's simply missing.
In this module you learn what Gate 7 runs and reports, then build and verify the evidence package for a period, a package that can prove all three.

6: Every lane writes the same record, Book 13's evidence record, with seven fields.
The guide shows where each comes from on these products.
Origin is the SailPoint trigger and workflow, the reconciliation finding, or the catalog request.
Owner and clock are the ServiceNow assignment, severity, priority and due date.
Approval is the ServiceNow or SailPoint approval.
Executing identity is the connector's or spoke's service principal, or a person's pim activation.
What ran is the provisioning event, the workflow version or the session recording.
Result is the re-read evidence, and closure is the closed record with its hash.
In Pass 1, three of those are empty: approval, executing identity and what ran.
Pass 1 doesn't actuate, so the record that would hold them is a later pass.
The export writes each as null, with that reason, rather than leaving the field out or filling it.
7: The re-read client from Module 6 already writes the evidence onto each record it closes: the evidence itself as canonical jay-son, its SHA-256 hash, the verification time, a close note and an attachment.
But nothing read the records back out.
It reads closed and cancelled findings through the Table A P I, under its own read-only role, and writes one record per finding in Book 13's shape.
Then it runs four checks on each, reported by name.
Does the evidence still hash to the stored hash?
If not, it was edited after closure, or cut short by the four-thousand-character field.
Does a closed record carry evidence at all?
If not, the close bypassed the business rule.
Does the evidence say the intended state matched?
And did it finish inside its response window, verified at or before its due date?
8: The export packages the period in three files.
Records dot J S O N L holds one record per line, and each line carries the SHA-256 of the line before it, so a removed or reordered record breaks the chain.
Summary dot jay-son holds window adherence, the count of declared exceptions and the records with problems.
And the manifest holds a SHA-256 for each file and the chain head.
The previous-manifest option continues last period's chain into this one.
The generated-at option fixes the timestamp, so the same records always give the same bytes.
And verify-dir recomputes every hash and walks the chain.
That's the check an I S S O runs on a package they receive.
One caution: the package is tamper-evident, not signed.
Anyone who can rewrite every file and the manifest can rewrite the chain.
So, as design guidance, keep each manifest where the exporter can't write, and sign it if the program requires.
9: Window adherence needs care, because it's easy to measure in a way that flatters.
Chapter 07 measures it the way Book 13 and Book 12's Chapter 12 define it: closures inside the window, over closures judged.
It isn't a ratio of open findings, which improves as new ones arrive.

The kit's fixture has five fictional closed records, one per case: one closed in its window, one closed late, one whose evidence was edited after it closed, one cancelled as a declared exception, and one closed with no evidence at all.
You'll export all five in the lab.
One thing wasn't verified: the format and time zone of the date values the Table A P I returns on a given instance.
The export parses both common forms, and Lab 2 checks yours.
10: Chapter 07 lists the dangers to the evidence, and the guard for each.
A record edited after closure would say something the re-read didn't, so the export recomputes the evidence hash and reports a mismatch.
Evidence cut short by the field length can't be parsed, so it's reported, and the attachment holds the full copy.
A close that bypassed the business rule is named: closed without re-read evidence.
A record deleted from the period would make the package look complete, but the chain breaks and the verifier reports it.
Fields filled in to look complete would claim an approval that never happened, so later-pass fields stay null with their reason, and tests pin that.
And if the export ran with the verifier's role, it could close findings, so it runs under its own read-only role, which the kit's call list can check.

12: Step four starts November's chain from October's head.
The export runs over the same fixture for period November, with the previous-manifest option pointing at October's manifest.
On the slide, its first five lines are trimmed, because they repeat step two.
The last line reports November's chain head, and November's manifest records October's head as its chain previous.
So a period can't be swapped out without breaking the next one.
Step five is the test that matters to an I S S O.
A one-line Python command deletes the second record from October's records file, and then you verify again.
The verifier finds two problems: the file's SHA-256 no longer matches the manifest, and the next line's previous hash no longer matches the line before it.
